title: John Donne
hookLine: a poet-dean: no man is an island; any man's death diminishes me

lines: A POET WHO BECAME A PRIEST.
cards: A man lies sick in bed in London, too ill to get up. Through the window comes a church bell, tolling slowly, the way a passing bell rang when someone in the parish was dying. He doesn't know who it's for.
Instead of finding out, he turns the thought over, and writes. That sick man had once written daring love poems, then became a priest and the dean of St Paul's Cathedral in London.
Out of that sickbed came a few lines that still turn up far from any church.

teach.b: John Donne wrote his Devotions during a serious illness: meditations, prayers and arguments with himself about sickness, death and God.
In one, he hears the bell and wonders whether it's tolling for someone he doesn't know, or, if he's sicker than he thinks, for himself.
Then comes this, in modern spelling: "No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main". The main is the mainland.
A little later: "any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind".
And he ends: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee." Donne uses man the way his century did, for every human being, which is why today's line says no one.

His point is sharper than a pleasant feeling of connection. In his view, a stranger's death actually takes something from each of us, because we're part of the same body of humankind. Some readers hear Paul behind it.

Paul describes the church as one body with many parts, in the King James Bible: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it."
Donne stretched that body wide. Every bell, every funeral, every name in the news is, in his picture, a clod of earth washed away by the sea.

how: Donne's words are read at funerals and memorial services, and in some parishes a bell is still tolled for the dead, with prayers for them.

o: a poet-priest who wrote from a sickbed that no one stands alone

games.q: you're lying sick in bed and hear a church bell tolling for someone in the parish who is dying. what do you do?
o: send someone to find out who died.
turn the thought over and write about it.
close the window to shut out the sound.
games.why: Donne turned it into writing: never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.

practice: Start with something close, the chair under you, your clothes, the last thing you ate, and ask quietly: who grew it, sewed it, drove it here?
Let the faces you'll never meet come to mind, and follow one thread back to the field, the factory, the ship, feeling yourself a piece of the continent.
If you pray, hold them all before God for a moment; if you don't, rest in being part of the main.

wordCard.voice: John Donne. A poet who became a priest and dean of St Paul's, who wrote from a sickbed that no one is an island, and that the tolling bell tolls for each of us.

orig.note: Greek: a member or limb of the body, the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 12 for each part of the one body.

carryVoice: Your line: no one is an island. The bell is never only for a stranger. Day eight hundred eighty-four.
